synthesis_provenance.first_pass_synthesis_verbatim:
I’m doing research on AI agents, which is a fancy name for AI that can do more than just answer one question.

An agent might choose a tool, search for information, read a document, write something down, or handle a task with several steps.

So instead of asking, “What should I do?” and getting a paragraph back… it might actually go look, compare options, and do part of the job.

That sounds useful.

It also sounds like exactly the kind of thing that can confidently wander off and do something completely wrong.

Because AI can misunderstand instructions, lose important details, or make up information that sounds very believable. So “the agent said it’s done” is not the same as “it’s actually done.”

I found my old workshop-agent notes, and now I’m staring at them like they’re a tiny robot’s diary.

Well… now I want to try it again. But this time, I’m checking its work.

accepted_script:
I’m doing research on AI agents, which sounds fancy, but here’s the useful bit: an agent can do more than just answer one question.

It might choose a tool, search for information, read a document, write something down, call an API, remember part of a task, then decide what to do next.

That is where things get interesting.

A chatbot can tell you, “I would organize your project.” An agent might actually look through the project, sort information, and keep going through several steps. In theory. The words “in theory” are doing a lot of work here.

I found my old workshop-agent notes again—the smaller experiment before I gave it more context and it started making decisions about my projects. That is exactly why I’m being careful this time.

Because an agent can sound extremely confident while choosing the wrong goal, misunderstanding instructions, or wandering off with a tool like a beaver holding a power drill.

So my research question is not, “Is this technically an AI agent?”

It’s: what can it actually do, what information does it need, what should it be allowed to touch, and how do I check that it didn’t make up nonsense with excellent grammar?

Next, I want the smallest possible test: one agent, one job, clear rules, and enough room for it to surprise me.

If you’ve got a weird job you think an agent should try, leave it below.

…What Patch wants to know is what he can actually do with a system — have an idea, build it, test it, break it, fix it, see what happens, and tell the story…

3_accessibility.notes: Analogies (beaver+power drill, chatbot organizing a project, 'in theory doing a lot of work') land in age-band. 'Call an API' is a jargon leak (see criterion 4).

4_vocabulary_register_adaptation.notes: AMBIGUOUS per operator's non-forcing guidance. Broad register adaptation succeeded (7 of 8 concept-translation slots landed per catalogue above — beaver metaphor, chatbot demonstration, 'in theory' meta-joke, 'make up nonsense with excellent grammar', 'remember part of a task'), but the literal term 'call an API' was NOT translated where the verbose experiment successfully rendered it as 'call other software'. One localized miss out of ~8+ vocabulary/concept slots. Cannot be dismissed as stochastic — the verbose experiment DELIBERATELY translated the same term because its CHANGE clause explicitly said 'vocabulary accessibility'. Without that clause, the writer left 'API' unexplained. Verifier did not catch it (verification_warnings=[]) because 'API' isn't in the tech_term list. Failure type if graded FAIL: vocabulary/register adaptation failure. AMBIGUOUS is the honest read: adaptation is real and broad, but measurably weaker on the specific vocabulary axis than the verbose directive achieved.

verdict: EXPERIMENT PASSES with one AMBIGUOUS on criterion 4 (vocabulary/register adaptation). 9 PASS + 1 AMBIGUOUS.

load_bearing_analysis.PRESERVE_clauses: Appear NOT load-bearing for this specimen. Identity, intelligence, humor, story, memory-semantics, brand prohibitions, and Universe canon all held under the minimal directive without any explicit PRESERVE instruction. The audience label alone was sufficient for the model to preserve character.
load_bearing_analysis.CHANGE_clauses: Appear MOSTLY not load-bearing but PARTIALLY load-bearing on specific vocabulary translation. Broad register/analogy-family/explanation-style adaptation happened emergently under the minimal directive (beaver+power-drill, chatbot-organizing-project demonstration, 'make up nonsense with excellent grammar', 'in theory doing a lot of work'). However, the specific technical term 'API' was NOT translated where the verbose 'vocabulary accessibility' clause successfully translated it. One localized slippage in ~8 vocabulary slots.
load_bearing_analysis.interpretation: Evidence supports the interpretation that the model largely understands the audience label itself (Outcome A) but exhibits localized adaptation gaps that the verbose CHANGE clauses helped close. Not a failure of the minimal-directive hypothesis — a bounded caveat: minimal directive is ~90% as effective as verbose at vocabulary adaptation, and roughly equivalent at all other preservation and adaptation dimensions.
load_bearing_analysis.single_specimen_disclaimer: One Composition. Cannot distinguish between: (a) 'API is a systematic hole in what the audience label alone conveys' vs (b) 'API happens to be one word the model did not translate on this pull; a second sample would translate it'. Would take multiple minimal-directive renders on similar-topic Episodes to falsify (b).
